Area.evidence_source: The participants in the study appeared to experience an absence of the all-important father–son relationship, therefore lacking a male role model whom they could be guided by in terms of their emotional self.I think this anxiety and apprehension was also to do with this lack of bonding with my dad; I felt vulnerable, no strong male role model, so I think that just kind of exacerbated the whole gay thing for me.... (Ben)Sometimes I felt that I wanted more approval from him . . . more affection, and certain things kind of hurt. We went on a Cub camp once, father and son.... there was a sort of an assault course thing, I fell over halfway through and he actually insisted that I should carry on and finish it and then he was really proud of me that I'd been a man. I don't know . . . to me it was a bit odd that I would have to do that to be able to earn his approval. (Ian)Regardless of the participants feeling they were not living up to the expectations of their fathers, they all continued to seek approval and love from them. The unmet need for parental love and approval appears to have led to self-harming behaviour.One strong incident that I can remember, I was 10, I remember being very angry with him [Dad] to the point that I put my fist through the kitchen window as he stood at the sink. I just thought I'm going to show you how angry I am . . . I can remember I wanted him to respond . . . a cry for his love ultimately. (Ben)Each of the participants was self-blaming in explaining the difficulties in their relationship with their father. Ben's talks of being 'afraid' of having physical contact with his father as he believes being gay will contaminate his father in some way:There was very little physical contact with me and my dad, and then when I was gay I think I became afraid then of physical contact with him . . . I remember thinking, if I touch him is he going to be thinking I'm touching him in some gay, sexualized way rather than thinking, well he is my father.... (Ben)As children, each of them needed parental approval and love and their father to be a role model. For the participants in this study, it appeared that their homosexuality eclipsed such opportunities, heightening their loneliness and their felt experience of being an outsider.
